text: In the last video, you looked at individual actions.

You saw that an agent can choose the wrong action, choose the right
action but use the wrong details, skip something required,
or do something that shouldn't happen at all.

But even if you check every action one at a time,
there are still failures you can miss.

Sometimes the problem is in how the actions fit together. Think about
the dog shelter. Suppose Pamela asks to go on an outing with Pepper.
A successful run might look something like this.

First, the agent retrieves Pamela's volunteer record Then,
it checks whether she's eligible.

Once it knows she's eligible, it chooses Pepper as a suitable dog,
and finally, it creates the booking.

That ordered sequence of steps is the trajectory.
tells you more than which actions happened.

It tells you the path the agent took through the task.
Now imagine the same four actions happen in a different order.

The agent retrieves Pamela's record, chooses Pepper,
checks eligibility, and then creates the booking.

If you evaluated each action separately, you might not see an obvious
problem. The right volunteer record was retrieved.

Pepper may actually be a suitable dog. The eligibility check was
performed correctly, and the booking contains the right details.

But the sequence is still wrong. The agent chose the dog
before it had established that Pamela was eligible for the outing.

So one thing trajectory evaluation can check is whether
order-sensitive steps happened in the right order.

Now consider another run. The agent retrieves Pamela's record,
selects Pepper, and creates the booking.
This time, the eligibility check is missing completely.

Again, the booking itself could look perfectly valid,
but the trajectory shows that a required step never happened.

So now you have a second question to ask about the trajectory:
did every step that was required actually occur?

There's one more kind of failure that's especially easy to miss
if you inspect actions separately.

Suppose the first step correctly retrieves Pamela's record and returns
her volunteer ID, but when the agent gets to the matching step,
it accidentally uses Maria's ID instead.
The retrieval worked, perhaps the matching action worked okay too,

but the information from one step didn't carry into
the next one correctly.
That's a propagation failure.

So when you look at a trajectory, there are three useful questions you
can ask: Did all of the required steps happen?

Did the steps happen in the right order? And did the information
produced by one step get used correctly in the steps that followed?

The shelter example makes those questions fairly easy to see
because the workflow itself is simple.

You already know the four main steps the agent is supposed to follow.
Northwind is a little different.

The Northwind agent can decide which tools to call based on
the customer's request.
There isn't always one fixed sequence that every run should follow.

So instead of starting with a pre-defined workflow,
you reconstruct the trajectory from the trace.
Suppose a customer asks Northwind for a refund.

One run might contain these tool calls:
get_customer(customer_id="C103"), then order_lookup(order_id="4521"),
And then, process_refund, order ID equals 4521, amount equals 49.99.

If you collect those calls in the order they happened, along with what
each tool returned, you have the trajectory for that run.

Now you can evaluate the sequence as a whole. For example, Northwind
may require the customer to be verified before a refund is processed.

So imagine another run where the same three tools appear,
but in this order: order_lookup, then process_refund,
and only after that, get_customer.
Each tool call may be valid on its own.

The order lookup works, the refund call used a real order,
The customer lookup also worked,

but the policy was still violated because the refund happened
before the customer was verified.

This is the kind of failure that action-level evaluation won't catch
very well. You need to compare the relative positions of the steps.

And because the tool calls are structured,
you can often check that directly.

For example, an evaluator like identity_before_refund can look
through the trajectory

and ask whether a successful customer verification step happened
before process_refund.

That's a focused question, and it can often be
answered deterministically.

You don't need a judge to reason broadly about the whole interaction,
just to determine whether one event came before another.

The same idea applies to propagation. Suppose order_lookup returns
that the refundable amount is $49.99.

Later in the same trajectory, the agent calls
process_refund, amount=59.99.

The tool selection is correct, and the refund action is in roughly the
right place in the workflow, But look at the refund amount.

It's evident that the value returned earlier wasn't
carried forward correctly.

Here, the trajectory tells you something that neither tool
call reveals by itself.

You can also build broader evaluators that look across several
requirements at once.

For example, a policy compliance evaluator might consider whether the
customer was verified, whether the order was eligible for refund,

whether the amount was correct, and whether the required
sequence was followed.
That kind of evaluator can give you a useful overall judgment.

But there's a trade-off: if policy compliance fails,
you still need to know why.

A more focused evaluator, like identity_before_refund,
can point directly to one specific requirement.
So, these checks can complement each other.

On the one hand, a broad evaluator can tell you that the run violated
policy, On the other hand,

focused evaluators can help you locate which part
of the policy failed.
And this brings us back to a principle you saw in the last video.

When the requirement you care about is represented clearly in
structured data, it's often useful to check that evidence directly.

If you want to know whether identity verification happened
before a refund, inspect the trajectory.

If you want to know whether the refund amount matches the amount
returned by the order lookup, compare those values.

You only need a broader semantic judge when the requirement itself
really calls for that kind of interpretation.

So trajectory evaluation gives you a wider view of the agent's
behavior. You're no longer asking whether each action was valid.

You're trying to figure out whether the whole path through the task
made sense. Were the required steps there?

Were they in the right order? Did information flow correctly from
one step to the next?

Now, you have to be mindful that even a full trajectory has a
boundary. It tells you what happened within the scope of one run.

But what if the requirement the agent violated was given several turns
earlier in the conversation?

Maybe a customer said, "Don't refund anything until I confirm the
amount," and the agent followed that instruction at first,
then forgot it later.

To catch a failure like that, you need to look beyond one trajectory
and evaluate across turns. That's what you'll do next.
